passage:
Saturday night
The class chat has been going crazy about Aadhya since afternoon. The screenshot, the laughing faces, the comments. I read every message. I didn't laugh. I felt sick, actually.
I typed "guys this is not okay" three times and deleted it three times. Because I know how it works. The second you defend someone, you're the next joke. Last year it was Pratik, just for one comment.
So I just watched. Forty-two people in the group and only eight are posting. The rest of us are like me, I bet. Quiet.
But when nobody says anything, it looks like everybody agrees. And Aadhya is seeing all of it.
Yash

qa.q: How many people are in the class chat?
qa.a: There are forty-two people in the group, and only eight are posting.

qa.q: What was Yash afraid of when deleting that message?
qa.a: Yash was afraid of becoming the next joke, like Pratik last year, if Yash defended Aadhya.

qa.q: What small step could Yash take at this stage?
qa.a: Yash could message Aadhya privately to show support, or quietly tell a trusted teacher, which does not make Yash a public target.

qa.q: What might Aadhya think on seeing the silence?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel the whole class believes the story, not knowing many readers feel uneasy too.

grounding: It shows a silent reader of a group chat who feels uneasy but stays quiet for fear of being targeted, while silence makes the rumour seem believed.

passage:
The Class 10 group chat of the government school in Sikar pinged forty times in an hour. Someone had written that Pinki had been seen at the bus stand "with a boy from the college", followed by a string of jokes.

Shreya read every message, lying on the charpai in the courtyard. Her stomach felt tight. Pinki sat next to her in maths. Pinki had cousins who were in college.

She typed, "This isn't nice." Then she deleted it. If she said anything, they would turn on her. They'd find something about her.

She scrolled down. Seventy-two people in the group. Only six were writing. The rest, like her, were reading. Kishore, who always had something to say, hadn't typed a word.

Shreya put the phone face down. She told herself she'd done nothing wrong. But it felt like the silence of all seventy-two made the story sound true.

qa.q: How many people were in the group chat?
qa.a: Seventy-two.

qa.q: Why did Shreya delete her message?
qa.a: She felt uneasy but afraid that if she spoke up, the group would turn on her and she'd be the next target.

qa.q: What small step could Shreya take that feels safer than posting?
qa.a: She could message Pinki privately with support, or tell a teacher or parent about the chat, instead of staying silent.

qa.q: How might Pinki experience seeing so many people read and say nothing?
qa.a: She would likely feel isolated and humiliated, as if everyone believed the story.

grounding: Shreya reads a rumour in the class chat and feels uneasy but stays silent for fear of becoming a target, making the rumour seem widely believed.

passage:
Nadia's school group chat in Nairobi was full of memes about Achieng. Someone said she'd been caught stealing from the tuck shop. Someone else posted a photo of her with a red circle around her bag.

Nadia read it on the matatu home. She didn't believe it. Achieng was one of the quietest girls in their year.

She looked at the member list: ninety-one people. Maybe eight were posting. Everyone else, like her, was just watching the messages scroll past.

She saw that Wanjiru, Achieng's own neighbour, had seen every message and said nothing.

Nadia's thumb hovered over the keyboard. What if they started on her next? She had a stammer they'd teased before.

She closed the app. On the matatu, a man was laughing into his phone, and Nadia felt suddenly, stupidly, like crying.

qa.q: How many people were in the group chat?
qa.a: Ninety-one.

qa.q: Why was Nadia afraid to type something?
qa.a: She was afraid that the group would start on her next, since they had teased her stammer before.

qa.q: What could Nadia do that doesn't make her a public target?
qa.a: Send Achieng a private kind message, or tell a teacher about the chat, so the silence doesn't leave Achieng alone.

qa.q: How might Achieng feel seeing that ninety-one people saw it and few objected?
qa.a: She would probably feel alone and ashamed, as if everyone believed the story.

grounding: Nadia reads a rumour in the school chat, feels uneasy but stays silent for fear of becoming the next target, like most of the group.

passage:
In the boys' hostel at the residential school in Dharwad, Kishore lay on his bunk after lights-out, reading the hostel group chat under his blanket.

Someone had posted that Jagdish, from the next dorm, cried every night for his mother. Then came the nicknames. Then a voice note of someone fake-sobbing.

Kishore's chest felt tight. Jagdish was new. He'd lent Kishore his torch on the first night.

Sixty-three people in the group. The same five kept posting. Kishore watched the little "seen by" count climb: 20, 35, 51. Nobody said stop.

He started to type, "Guys, leave him." Then he thought of the older boys who ran the group. Last term they'd made a boy's life miserable for a month.

He deleted it. So did, he suspected, a lot of others. And the silence made it look like everyone agreed.

qa.q: What did Jagdish lend Kishore on the first night?
qa.a: His torch.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel as the "seen by" count climbed?
qa.a: His chest felt tight; he felt uneasy and sorry for Jagdish, but afraid of the older boys.

qa.q: What could Kishore do the next morning?
qa.a: Tell the hostel warden about the chat and quietly check on Jagdish, so he isn't left alone and the group isn't the only voice.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jagdish to see the "seen by" count with no one objecting?
qa.a: He would probably feel lonely and humiliated, as if the whole hostel agreed with the jokes.

grounding: In a hostel chat, Kishore feels uneasy about a rumour but stays silent for fear of becoming the next target, and the silence makes it look believed.

passage:
Dear Kiran Didi,
Something's been bothering me and I can't say it at home. Our class group has been going wild since Monday. Asif posted that Priyanka copied in the chemistry test, and now people keep adding "proof": a blurry photo, a "someone saw her".
Sixty-two people are in that group. I've read every message. So have most of us, I think; you can see the little seen-by list. Nobody has written, "This isn't fair." I typed it twice and deleted it twice. I kept thinking, if I say something, next week it'll be me.
But when nobody says anything, it looks as if all sixty-two of us believe it. Priyanka sits two seats from me. She hasn't looked up in class for two days.
What would you do?
Tanuja

qa.q: How many people are in the class group?
qa.a: Sixty-two people are in that group.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja type 'This isn't fair' and then delete it twice?
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy about the rumour but scared of becoming the next target by speaking up.

qa.q: What small step could Tanuja take that doesn't mean confronting the whole group?
qa.a: Tanuja could message Priyanka privately to show support, refuse to forward anything, and tell a teacher as well as Kiran Didi what is happening.

qa.q: What is it like for Priyanka while the group stays silent?
qa.a: Priyanka seems isolated and ashamed, not looking up for two days, and the silence may make it seem to her that everyone believes the story.

grounding: Shows a classmate reading a rumour in a group chat, feeling uneasy but staying silent out of fear, and how that silence makes the rumour look believed.
